claim: In its order delivered on Saturday 28 November 2026, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea prescribes at least one provisional measure in Argentina's case against the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project.

runs.reason:
**Base rate.** In the eight previous ITLOS proceedings I count that reached an Article 290(5) order, the Tribunal prescribed at least one measure in all eight, counting the joined *Southern Bluefin Tuna* cases once. That is a strong starting point, but a small sample. The most relevant precedents are *MOX Plant* (December 3, 2001) and *Land Reclamation* (October 8, 2003): in both, ITLOS prescribed cooperation and consultation rather than granting the requested halt. Either kind of operative measure would count here. ([itlos.org](https://www.itlos.org/en/main/cases/list-of-cases/))

**What moves this case away from the base rate.**
- **Down — jurisdiction.** On November 10, the UK argued that Argentina’s claimed rights over the Sea Lion site depend on who has sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. That is a more substantial obstacle than the one in *Ghana/Côte d’Ivoire*, where the dispute was about delimiting maritime entitlements from undisputed land territory. Even a narrow order needs a prima facie basis for jurisdiction. ([itlos.org](https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/cases/37/PV/ITLOS_PV26_C37_2_E_checked.pdf))
- **Down — urgency.** On November 10, the UK confirmed that drilling would not start before March 21, 2027, or extraction before March 2028. On November 11, it argued that the Annex VII tribunal could act on an interim request by January 2027. That timetable is not assured, but if ITLOS accepts it, the Tribunal can decline relief or record the UK’s assurances without prescribing anything. November 20 reporting on contractor replacements gave no indication that drilling would move forward. ([itlos.org](https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/cases/37/PV/ITLOS_PV26_C37_2_E_checked.pdf))
- **Up — there is a narrower route to YES.** Argentina’s November 11 final submissions raised marine-environment and information issues alongside drilling. If ITLOS sees a dispute over environmental obligations that it can address without deciding sovereignty, a binding consultation or information-sharing measure is more plausible than a drilling freeze. ([itlos.org](https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/cases/37/PV/C37_final_submissions_Arg_Eng.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Exact-date risk.** ITLOS formally announced a public reading at noon Hamburg time on Saturday, November 28. I put the chance of no delivery in the specified window at about **2%**. The main reason to favor NO is the combination of jurisdiction and urgency, not the Saturday sitting. ([itlos.org](https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/press_releases_english/PR_405_en.pdf?utm_source=openai))

COUNTER  
ITLOS could treat marine-environment cooperation as an UNCLOS issue distinct from sovereignty and find that waiting for the Annex VII tribunal leaves a gap in protection. Its *MOX Plant* and *Land Reclamation* orders show that it can fill that gap with binding consultation or information sharing without halting the project. ([itlos.org](https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/cases/37/PV/C37_final_submissions_Arg_Eng.pdf?utm_source=openai))

This heavily undermines the urgency for halting Sea Lion now, and increases the probability that ITLOS either places the UK's 21 March 2027 assurance on record without prescribing measures, or rejects the request for lack of urgency prior to constitution of the arbitral panel.

**3. Strongest Reason the More Likely Outcome Might Fail**
Evaluating the competing considerations, the more likely outcome (narrowly) is **NO** (that ITLOS declines to prescribe provisional measures, either because the core dispute concerns land sovereignty outside UNCLOS prima facie jurisdiction, or because the UK's binding assurance of no drilling before 21 March 2027 removes any urgency prior to the January 2027 constitution of the Annex VII tribunal, leading the Tribunal merely to record the assurance and reject the request). The strongest reason this outcome might fail is ITLOS's unbroken historical practice in Article 290(5) environmental cases (*MOX Plant* and *Land Reclamation*): even when ITLOS found that the short timeframe before the constitution of the Annex VII tribunal meant there was no urgency to halt the industrial activity itself, the Tribunal still found prima facie jurisdiction under Part XII (Articles 192 and 194) and used its *proprio motu* authority to *prescribe* a formal provisional measure in the *dispositif* ordering the parties to cooperate, consult, exchange environmental information, or avoid aggravating the dispute. There is also a negligible (<1%) chance of an unforeseen procedural delay postponing delivery past 28 November 2026.

COUNTER
In every prior Article 290(5) request that reached an order, ITLOS has found prima facie jurisdiction and prescribed at least one provisional measure, even when it declined to halt the challenged project for lack of immediate urgency. Specifically, following its precedents in *MOX Plant* and *Land Reclamation*, the Tribunal could bypass the territorial sovereignty question by finding prima facie jurisdiction over Argentina's marine environment claims under Articles 192 and 194 of UNCLOS, and prescribe a measure of its own motion ordering the parties to exchange environmental information, consult, or refrain from aggravating the dispute pending the arbitration.

facts.fact: Argentina submitted a request to ITLOS under Article 290(5) of UNCLOS for the prescription of four provisional measures against the United Kingdom to prevent hydrocarbon exploitation in the Sea Lion project and protect the marine environment under Articles 192 and 194, following its 28 September 2026 notification instituting Annex VII arbitration.

In a cover note dated 2 November 2026 and published by ITLOS, the United Kingdom stated it would ask the Tribunal to reject Argentina's request in its entirety on the grounds that the Annex VII tribunal lacks prima facie jurisdiction, the alleged rights are not plausible, and there is no urgency or risk of irreparable prejudice, submitting witness statements from Jack Ford MLA, Navitas CEO Ian Ramsay, and Rockhopper CEO Samuel Moody.

According to the verbatim record of the ITLOS hearing on 10 November 2026 (ITLOS/PV.26/C37/2), the United Kingdom told the Tribunal that both parties had already appointed their arbitrators, that the 60-day period to agree on the remaining members expires on 27 November 2026 so the Annex VII tribunal will be constituted by January 2027 at the latest, and that drilling in the Sea Lion field is scheduled to commence no earlier than 21 March 2027.

At the close of oral proceedings in Hamburg on 11 November 2026, Argentina submitted its final submissions requesting four provisional measures, including that the United Kingdom ensure no new drilling for exploitation and no installation of production infrastructure takes place in the North Malvinas Basin in connection with the Sea Lion project.
On 11 November 2026, the Agent for the United Kingdom submitted final submissions inviting ITLOS to reject all requests by the Argentine Republic for the prescription of provisional measures.

On 18 November 2026, ITLOS issued press release ITLOS/Press 405 announcing that the Tribunal will deliver its Order in Case No. 37 at a public sitting on Saturday, 28 November 2026, at noon Hamburg time.

Specifically, following its precedents in *MOX Plant* and *Land Reclamation*, the Tribunal could bypass the territorial sovereignty question by finding prima facie jurisdiction over Argentina's marine environment claims under Articles 192 and 194 of UNCLOS, and prescribe a measure of its own motion ordering the parties to exchange environmental information, consult, or refrain from aggravating the dispute pending the arbitration.

runs.reason:
The order is fixed for delivery on 28 November 2026 and has not yet been issued. Historically, ITLOS has prescribed at least one provisional measure in every Article 290(5) case that reached an order after a hearing, often adding cooperation, information-exchange, or non-aggravation measures of its own motion even when it refused the applicant’s main request. Full refusals have been confined mainly to Article 290(1) cases in which urgency or irreparable prejudice was not shown.

Two features of this case pull strongly away from that base rate. First, Article 290(5) authorizes measures only for the short interval before the Annex VII tribunal is constituted. At the hearing the United Kingdom stated that the parties were already meeting on the remaining appointments, that the arbitral tribunal should be seated by the end of 2026 or January 2027 at the latest, that drilling will not begin before 21 March 2027, and that extraction will not begin before March 2028. If those facts are accepted, the urgency condition fails, and the usual disposition is to reject the request (often while placing the statements on record). Second, the claim is tightly bound to sovereignty over the Falkland Islands/Malvinas, which lies outside UNCLOS dispute settlement; a finding of no prima facie jurisdiction is an independent ground for rejection. Either ground, without a paragraph that prescribes a measure, resolves the claim NO.

ITLOS has prescribed at least one provisional measure in every Article 290(5) case decided after a hearing, frequently adding a cooperation or non-aggravation measure of its own motion even when it refused the applicant’s principal request.
